newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgarian parliament approves Videnov resignation.
newsitem.headline: Bulgarian parliament approves Videnov resignation.

text.p: Bulgaria's parliament on Saturday approved the resignation of Prime Minister Zhan Videnov, but opposition deputies pressing for early elections protested against the ruling Socialists' intention to form a new cabinet.

Videnov tendered his resignation and that of his cabinet at a party congress last Saturday, saying he felt he lacked the support he needed from the party and the country to continue as prime minister and party leader.
According to the constitution, Videnov's cabinet remains in power until the ruling Bulgarian Socialist Party (BSP) forms a new cabinet which should be approved by parliament next month.
The resignation received 211 votes in favour, three votes against, and nine abstentions.

Opposition deputies walked out of a second vote on whether the outgoing cabinet should introduce to parliament a draft 1997 budget, a new privatisation programme and legal amendments for the introduction of a currency board fixed exchange rate regime, allowing parliament to vote on them by mid-January.

"This government has shown that it is inept in drafting budgets, and why should we be burdened by yet another unrealistic budget after this cabinet is gone," said opposition deputy Ventsisav Dimitrov.
Videnov's cabinet has revised this year's budget three times to accommodate growing spending on domestic debt and subsidies to loss-making state enterprises.
On Tuesday, the Socialist party congress elected Georgi Parvanov to replace Videnov as party leader, a choice seen as a compromise between party reformists and hardliners.

A new prime minister must negotiate with the International Monetary Fund (IMF) on introduction of a currency board, and withstand criticism of the initial hardship exected to accompany its implementation.

Possible premiers include the speaker of parliament Blagovest Sendov, seen as another compromise candidate, and U.S.-born former foreign minister Georgi Pirinski, who resigned after a party confidence vote gave Videnov only narrow backing last month.

"I hope the Bulgarian people will not be punished for their patience by yet another government composed of former communists," opposition deputy and former prime minister Filip Dimitrov told parliament.

Dimitrov repeated opposition calls for early elections to produce a government of "a more realistic majority". Opposition candidate Petar Stoyanov defeated Socialist Culture Minister Ivan Marazov to win last month's presidential elections.

The BSP was formed by leading ex-communists who renamed the party after Zhivkov's overthrow in 1989. Its critics accuse it of being more interested in supporting its powerful business allies than in pushing through badly-needed economic reforms.

Videnov's government is half-way through its four-year term. Failure to carry out reforms such as closing loss-making state firms has led to suspension of funding from the World Bank and IMF, who support the currency board as a last chance to save the economy from disaster.

Under the mechanism, local currency in circulation must exactly match central bank reserves, which would halt the slide of the lev, restore confidence in the economy and remove political pressure to print money.
